content:
Ask ChatGPT "what's the WiFi password in our office" and it'll either make something up with full confidence, or admit it has no clue. Ask it about a court ruling from last month, or what's actually written in the PDF you just dragged into the chat, same story.

That's not because the model is dumb. It's because of how it actually works under the hood, and once you see that, the difference between a chatbot, an LLM, and a RAG system stops being marketing jargon and becomes obvious.

LLM vs Chatbot vs RAG, what's actually different

An LLM is the brain. It got trained once, on a giant snapshot of text up to some cutoff date, and that's it, frozen forever after. Ask it something and it answers from whatever patterns got baked into its weights during training, the same way you'd answer from memory of something you read two years ago: confident, often right, occasionally wrong, and definitely not aware of anything that happened since.

A chatbot is just that same frozen brain wearing a conversation UI. ChatGPT in its rawest form is exactly this, an LLM with a text box on top. Nothing about the underlying knowledge changes.

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) keeps the same frozen LLM, but before it answers, it sends someone to go fetch the actual relevant pages from a real source first, your documents, your notes, your company wiki, and hands those pages to the LLM along with your question. The model then answers from what it just read, not from what it vaguely remembers.

Simplest way to put it: a plain LLM is a closed-book exam, RAG is an open-book exam. Same student, wildly different accuracy, because one of them is allowed to look things up.

Why bother? Why not just train a bigger LLM?

A few reasons this doesn't go away just by scaling the model up:

  • Hallucination the model fills gaps in its memory with something that sounds plausible, because that's literally what it was trained to do, predict the next plausible word, not look anything up.
  • Knowledge cutoff the model genuinely cannot know about anything after its training data was collected, no matter how big it is.
  • Private data it was never trained on your company's internal docs, your Obsidian vault, or your unpublished research, and it never will be, that data isn't public.
  • Retraining is expensive fine-tuning a model every time a document changes is slow and costly. Updating a database of documents is instant.

RAG sidesteps all four. Keep the LLM frozen and dumb about your specific world, but hand it fresh, relevant, private context exactly when it needs it.

The actual flow, no chat UI, just the engine

Strip away the web app and the chat bubbles and a RAG system is really just two pipelines that run at completely different times.

Phase 1: Indexing (runs once, or whenever your documents change) 

Documents (markdown notes, PDFs, code, etc.)
   |
   v
Chunking            -> split into smaller overlapping pieces
   |
   v
Embedding model     -> turns each chunk into a vector of numbers
   |
   v
Vector Database     -> stores those vectors so they can be searched by similarity
Phase 2: Retrieval + Generation (runs every time someone asks a question) 

User query
   |
   v
Embed the query (same embedding model as indexing)
   |
   v
Search the vector DB for similar chunks   (semantic / dense search)
   +
Search a keyword index for exact matches  (BM25 / sparse search)
   |
   v
Merge both ranked lists into one (Reciprocal Rank Fusion)
   |
   v
Rerank the top candidates with a heavier, more accurate model
   |
   v
Stuff the top-k chunks into the LLM's prompt, alongside the question
   |
   v
LLM generates an answer grounded in those chunks

Step 1: Chunking, why you can't just dump the whole document in

LLMs have a finite context window, and even when they don't, stuffing an entire 50-page document in just to answer one question buries the relevant sentence in a haystack of irrelevant ones, wastes tokens, and makes retrieval imprecise. So before anything gets embedded, documents get split into smaller chunks first, and retrieval happens at the chunk level, not the document level.

The chunk size is a real trade-off. Too small and a chunk loses the surrounding context that gave it meaning (a sentence like "it returns -1 on failure" is useless without knowing what function it's talking about). Too big and you're back to the noisy-haystack problem, plus you waste context budget on irrelevant filler once it's retrieved.

Overlap exists to fix a specific failure mode: if you slice a document into clean, non-overlapping blocks, you will inevitably cut a key sentence exactly in half at a chunk boundary, where half the meaning ends up in chunk N and the other half in chunk N+1, and neither chunk alone is useful. So instead chunks are built like a sliding window with a stride smaller than the window itself, e.g. 500-token chunks with a 50-100 token overlap, so the tail end of one chunk reappears as the head of the next. 


def chunk_text(text, chunk_size=500, overlap=75):
    tokens = tokenize(text)
    chunks = []
    start = 0
    while start < len(tokens):
        end = start + chunk_size
        chunks.append(detokenize(tokens[start:end]))
        start += chunk_size - overlap   # step forward less than a full chunk
    return chunks

Common strategies beyond plain fixed-size slicing: splitting on sentence boundaries so you never cut mid-sentence, or recursive splitting that respects document structure first (markdown headers, paragraphs) and only falls back to raw token slicing if a section is still too big. For something like a vault of markdown notes, structure-aware splitting tends to keep chunks far more coherent than blind token counting.

Step 2: Turning text into numbers, embeddings and semantic search

An embedding model takes a piece of text and outputs a vector, a fixed-length list of numbers, such that chunks with similar meaning end up close together in that vector space, regardless of the exact words used. This is what makes semantic search possible: search by meaning, not by matching characters. A query for "puppy" can retrieve a chunk that only ever says "dog," because the model learned that those two concepts live near each other in vector space, something a plain keyword search could never do.

The standard way to measure "how close" two vectors are is cosine similarity, the cosine of the angle between them: 


cosine_similarity(A, B) = (A · B) / (||A|| * ||B||)

It only cares about direction, not magnitude, two vectors pointing the same way score close to 1 even if one is "longer" than the other. That scale-invariance is exactly why it's preferred over raw distance for comparing embeddings, you don't want a chunk to look less relevant just because it happened to produce a vector with bigger numbers.

For this kind of system, the embedding model matters a lot, it's literally defining what "similar" means. BAAI/bge-m3 is a solid pick here, it's multilingual, handles long passages well, and (the interesting part) can output dense embeddings, sparse term weights, and multi-vector representations all from the same model, which matters again once you get to hybrid search.

Step 3: Where do these vectors actually live? Why not a normal database

A normal SQL database is built around indexes like B-trees and hash indexes, and those are extremely good at exact-match lookups and range queries on structured, low-dimensional data, "find the row where id = 42." They were never built to answer "find me the 5 closest vectors to this one, out of 10 million, in 1024-dimensional space." Brute-force comparing your query against every single stored vector is O(N) per query, and at real scale that's just too slow.

Vector databases instead use Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search. The most common algorithm behind this is HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs), a layered graph where the top layer has very few nodes with long-range connections, and each layer below gets denser with more short-range connections, all the way down to a layer containing every vector. A search starts at the sparse top layer, greedily jumps toward the query, and drops down a layer once it can't get any closer, narrowing in on the right neighborhood in roughly logarithmic time instead of scanning everything. It trades a small amount of accuracy (it's "approximate," not exhaustive) for a massive speedup.

ChromaDB is a good example here, lightweight, runs locally, and uses HNSW under the hood for exactly this kind of similarity search.

Step 4: One retriever isn't enough, hybrid search

Dense embedding search is great at meaning, but it can genuinely miss exact terms it doesn't represent well, an error code like ECONNREFUSED, a specific person's name, a product SKU. A plain keyword search (the sparse, lexical kind, commonly done with BM25) nails those instantly, but it has the opposite blind spot, it has no idea that "car" and "automobile" mean the same thing.

So most real systems run both searches in parallel, one dense vector search and one sparse keyword search, then merge the two ranked lists into a single ranking. The merging step turns out to be more subtle than it sounds, because a BM25 score and a cosine similarity score live on completely different scales, you can't just add them together and expect anything sane. That whole mechanic, plus the full BM25 formula and the math behind merging rankings fairly, is exactly what Part 2 digs into.

Step 5: Reranking, a second, smarter pass

The first retrieval pass (BM25 + vector search) has to be fast across potentially millions of chunks, so it relies on a bi-encoder setup, the query gets encoded into a vector once, every chunk was already encoded independently ahead of time, and you just compare vectors. Cheap, but the query and the document never actually "see" each other, there's no interaction between them.

A reranker fixes that, but only on the shortlist. It takes the top 20-50 candidates from the first pass and feeds the query and each candidate chunk into the model together, as a single input, using a cross-encoder. The model can now directly attend across both texts at once and produce a much more accurate relevance score, at the cost of being far too slow to run on the entire dataset. That's exactly why it only ever touches the shortlist, never the full corpus. BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 is a common cross-encoder choice for this step.

Step 6: Finally, talking to the LLM

After reranking, you're left with a small, high-confidence set of chunks. Those get formatted into a prompt, system instructions plus the retrieved chunks plus the user's original question, and only then does the LLM generate an answer. The model isn't reasoning from memory anymore, it's reasoning over text that was handed to it seconds ago. That's the entire trick.

Putting it all together

Stage What it solves Example
Chunking + overlap Keeps retrieval precise without losing boundary context 500-token chunks, 75-token overlap
Dense (embeddings) Semantic / meaning-based matching "puppy" matches a chunk about "dog"
Sparse (BM25) Exact keyword / jargon matching Error codes, names, IDs
Vector DB (HNSW) Fast nearest-neighbor search at scale Sub-linear search over millions of chunks
Fusion + Reranking Combines both retrievers, then sharpens precision Top 50 candidates -> top 5 final chunks

Coming up in Part 2

This post deliberately stayed at the "what and why" level. Part 2 goes under the hood of the retrieval math itself: term frequency and why raw counts are a bad relevance signal on their own, the full TF-IDF formula, the complete BM25 formula broken term by term (what k1 and b actually control), the score-vs-term-frequency curve and what stays constant as a term repeats forever, why Reciprocal Rank Fusion beats naively adding scores together, and dense vs sparse vectors as actual mathematical objects rather than just "keyword search vs meaning search."

Further Reading

  • Pinecone's RAG learning series, a solid practical walkthrough of the pipeline
  • HNSW explained, for the vector DB internals
  • BAAI's FlagEmbedding repo, for the bge-m3 and bge-reranker model details
